title: Nvidia in 5 Years: Where the Stock Could Be Headed - The Motley Fool
content: The last five years saw shareholders grow their wealth by 1,000%. When investors talk about artificial intelligence (AI), Nvidia (NVDA +0.97%) might be the first business that comes to mind. There's a good reason for that. In the past five years, its shares have climbed 1,000%. Because the company is a critical provider of AI hardware, it will continue to capture the market's attention. The AI infrastructure build-out is in full swing and Nvidia has benefited more than any other company as the major hyperscalers are in a race to build more data centers. Nvidia Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress has estimated that combined capital expenditures will total "nearly $800 billion in 2026." The upward trajectory is unmistakable. The largest cost component of these facilities is the graphics processing units that Nvidia specializes in, with Vera Rubin being the latest platform. Nvidia has over 80% share of the market for data center chips. It has, unsurprisingly, registered eye-popping demand in recent years that has driven its financials to new heights. Nvidia reported $96.2 billion of revenue in its fiscal second quarter (ended July 26), a figure that rose 106% year over year. And its net income was up 126%. Pricing power has been a notable contributor to these numbers. According to analyst estimates, Nvidia's revenue is set to grow at a compound annual rate of 61% between fiscal 2026 and fiscal 2029, which will close in early 2029. Furthermore, its diluted earnings per share are projected to rise at a yearly clip of 65% during that time. These metrics present an incredibly powerful tailwind that can lift the stock higher. Nvidia is worth $5.5 trillion, and that market capitalization makes it the world's most valuable company. Investors are probably wondering if there's any upside left. What might be going on in late 2031, for example? To ponder that, first, consider the stock's valuation. This "Magnificent Seven" stock trades at a forward price-to-earnings ratio of only 25. That's 27% more expensive than the S&P 500 index. Given that Nvidia's earnings growth is astronomically higher than the benchmark's  average, that is a gap worth highlighting. The valuation isn't much higher because the market is questioning the durability of Nvidia's monster success. There is no telling how long the AI boom will last. While Nvidia's stock could easily be a double (and potentially a lot more) in five years if the momentum holds up, that outcome is full of extreme uncertainty. title: Nvidia Is Using Its Cash to Build the Next Generation of AI Customers - TradingView
content: The AI chipmaker, Nvidia Corp. (NVDA, Financials), is building out its presence in Europe by investing in French technology businesses that might be major consumers of artificial intelligence. Nvidia agreed to purchase a minority share in Doctolib, but the business did not reveal the size or value of the transaction. The healthcare technology business said it was working with Nvidia to build new AI solutions. Nvidia was also verified by Genesis AI as a strategic investor. These actions are tiny in relation to Nvidia's semiconductor business, but the approach is worth tracking. Increasingly, the company has been relying on investments and partnerships to build up the wider ecosystem around its hardware and software. It can take interests in startups producing AI products to have an earlier position in sectors that might later demand greater processing power. The investments also extend Nvidia's presence outside data centers.The acquisition provides the corporation another toehold in healthcare technology, while Genesis AI adds to its increasing collection of software-focused assets. A French tabloid also alleged that Nvidia had taken holdings in Entalpic and Pigment but the firms have not verified the deals. The next thing to monitor is whether Nvidia can transform these minority investments into deeper commercial agreements that will enhance demand for its processors, software and AI infrastructure throughout Europe. title: Nvidia Stocks Fall as Copenhagen Adds a Blackwell Deployment - TradingView
content: Nvidia, the AI-computing and networking supplier NVDA, secured another planned Blackwell deployment through Scaleway's Copenhagen expansion, according to Reuters on October 13. Shares traded at $225.67, down 0.3%, at 10:29 a.m. ET. The project adds another European destination for Nvidia's hardware. But without a disclosed order value or system count, investors have little basis to calculate its contribution to sales. The hardware packs plenty of muscle. Scaleway selected HGX B300, and Nvidia's documentation specifies eight Blackwell GPUs per baseboard, each carrying 288GB of memory. That totals 2.304TB of GPU memory per baseboard. Those specifications explain the computing capacity of each unit. They do not reveal the size of Scaleway's purchase. For investors, the missing numbers matter more than another impressive specification sheet. Nvidia's GF Score of 95 out of 100 shows strong profitability and growth, while the weaker GF Value reading makes valuation the clear pressure point. That is the tension here: a powerful business can still carry a demanding price. European demand for locally hosted AI computing could widen Nvidia's customer base, but the next useful evidence is concreteinstallation volumes, launch dates and follow-up orders. More deployment locations support the growth story; the dollars will determine how much this project matters. Select market data provided by ICE Data Services. title: 2X Nvidia ETFs Are Supposed to Double Daily Gains—Why Did Some Lag NVDA? - TradingView
content: Nvidia Corp. NVDA gained 34.8% between Sep. 5, 2025, and Oct. 12, 2026, but investors seeking amplified exposure through daily leveraged ETFs experienced markedly different outcomes. Morningstar Research Managing Director Jeffrey Ptak highlighted the disparity in a recent post on X, noting that 2x daily NVDA ETFs returned between 31.8% and 39.5% over the period. The nearly 8-percentage-point gap separated the best performer, Direxion’s fund, from the worst, T-REX’s offering. Here's the same thing, but this time for NVDA. NVDA rose 34.8% from 9/5/25 – 10/12/26. The 2x daily ETFs tracking it rose between 31.8% and 39.5% over that span. Again, surprisingly wide (~8 percentage points per year) gap between best (Direxion) and worst (T-Rex) performer. https://t.co/NRVBlwPWPs pic.twitter.com/t7V1Rxdvnw The comparison raises a question: If these ETFs all target twice Nvidia’s daily performance, why did their returns diverge so widely over the same period? The performance spread is striking because both products seek to deliver 200% of Nvidia’s daily stock return before fees and expenses. Direxion Daily NVDA Bull 2X ETF NVDU has an annual expense ratio of 0.92%, while the T-REX 2X Long NVIDIA Daily Target ETF (NASDAQ:NVDX) charges 1.05%, according to their published fund disclosures. That 0.13-percentage-point difference in annual expenses is unlikely, by itself, to explain a 7.7-percentage-point return gap over roughly 13 months. Other factors, including daily compounding, financing costs, portfolio implementation and tracking differences, warrant examination. The precise contribution of each factor cannot be established from the headline returns alone. The funds also differ in size. GraniteShares 2x Long NVDA Daily ETF NVDL has approximately $3.5 billion in net assets, compared with $523 million for NVDU and $442 million for NVDX. Why 2X NVDA ETFs Don’t Deliver Twice the Stock’s Return The critical distinction is that leveraged ETFs target a multiple of a stock’s daily return, not its cumulative return over several months or a year. To maintain that daily target, funds rebalance their exposure as Nvidia’s share price changes. Returns then compound from one trading session to the next, making the path of the stock’s gains and losses important. Consider a simplified example. If Nvidia rises 10% in one session and falls 10% the next, the stock loses 1% over the two sessions. A hypothetical 2x daily ETF would gain 20% on the first day and lose 20% on the second, leaving it down 4% before fees and other costs. This is why multiplying Nvidia’s 34.8% cumulative gain by two would produce a misleading benchmark. A 69.6% gain is not what a 2x daily ETF promises over the entire period. The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission warns that leveraged ETFs can diverge significantly from their stated multiples over periods longer than one day, particularly when markets are volatile. Ptak’s comparison also highlights why investors should not treat leveraged ETFs tracking the same stock as interchangeable. Expense ratios matter, but so do daily tracking performance, financing and derivative costs, distributions, and the difference between returns calculated using net asset value and exchange-traded market prices. A thorough comparison should use the same dates, return methodology and treatment of distributions for every fund. Traders considering leveraged Nvidia exposure should examine how consistently each product meets its daily objective, how much it costs to maintain exposure and how it behaves through both rallies and sharp reversals. With single-stock leverage amplifying Nvidia’s already concentrated risk, a strong underlying stock performance does not automatically translate into a superior long-term result for every 2x ETF. Driven by seemingly insatiable infrastructure demand from cloud titans, investors are treating NVDA as a surefire bet. Yet, beneath this euphoria lies a dangerous market asymmetry. As capital aggressively crowds into a handful of priced-to-perfection tech giants, exceptional value is being left behind in the wreckage of neglected sectors. While the market gladly pays extreme multiples for future AI promises, it is completely ignoring cash-generating machines hiding in plain sight—such as dating app pioneer Bumble (BMBL), which recently traded at a microscopic 2 times free cash flow. My name is Inan Dogan. I am Insider Monkey's cofounder and research director. I publish my personal stock picks in Insider Monkey's monthly premium newsletters. In February I finally pulled the trigger and added Bumble (BMBL) to our monthly newsletter's portfolio. Bumble was trading at 2 times free cash flow at the time. Its stock price was $2.75 at the time. I summarized my thesis as follows: "Bumble (BMBL) is currently significantly undervalued, trading at a "deep value" entry point following its massive post-IPO correction. I believe that the company's strong brand moat and high free cash flow generation provide a coiled-spring setup for a 300-400% recovery as management successfully executes its turnaround over the next few years. Bumble's stock price is finally cheap enough to provide an asymmetric risk-return opportunity. We don't know the exact figures for the entire 2025, but BMBL generated $182 million in free cash flow during the first 3 quarters. The total figure should be around $240 million. In late 2025, Bumble made a strategic move to purchase all outstanding TRA rights for $186 million in cash. While this was a significant one-time cash outlay, it eliminated a long-term liability and is expected to significantly improve the company's future cash flow profile by removing annual payment obligations. As of September 30, 2025, Bumble held $307.9 million in cash and equivalents against $589.4 million in total debt. If we add $60 million in free cash flow in Q4 and subtract the $186 million cash payment, we arrive at a total cash position of around $180 million. This means BMBL's net debt is around $410 million at the end of 2026. Basically we are buying the entire company (including its debt) at 3-4 times its cash flow." Today, Bumble disclosed that Ithaca Holdings will pay $6.05 per share. This is another Insider Monkey stock pick that more than doubled within a year (in this case 8 months). A year ago, I added Teva Pharmaceutical (TEVA) to our portfolio at $20. That stock is trading at $41 right now. We exited TEVA after an 80% gain earlier this year. We usually add one stock to our portfolio every month, so it isn't like we are picking dozens of stocks and BMBL and TEVA are cherry picked. Don't get me wrong. I believe AI is the most transformative technology ever. It is bigger than the industrial revolution and a large portion of our newsletter's portfolio is AI stocks, but not overpriced AI stocks. title: Nvidia's $4 Trillion 2030 Projection Makes It the Best Buy in the Market - The Motley Fool
content: Nvidia has a bold call for 2030, and it indicates huge growth ahead. Nvidia (NVDA +0.97%) is no stranger to making bold calls, and its visionary CEO Jensen Huang has made many of them in his time. However, this may be the boldest one yet. Over the past year, he has repeatedly told investors that the company expects up to $4 trillion in data center capital expenditures annually by 2030. The low end of that range is $3 trillion, so there is still a ton of growth ahead in this industry. While that may seem like a wild and far-off projection, it's likely not. Nvidia has more information about the trends of the artificial intelligence (AI) computing market than most investors, and sometimes it's better to let the experts do the talking for you and then invest based on what they say. Nvidia is the primary AI computing unit supplier to customers of all shapes and sizes. Its graphics processing units (GPUs) and the various products that support them are synonymous with AI computing, and every new AI computing device that launches is immediately compared to Nvidia's products. That's a great spot to be in, and Nvidia just raised the bar once again with its new Vera Rubin chip architecture. This will keep Nvidia in the driver's seat and allow it to issue bold calls like the $3 trillion to $4 trillion call it issued. None of the AI hyperscalers are getting as much computing power as they want, and many are seriously compute-constrained right now. Several of the cloud computing giants have a backlog totaling $500 billion or more, and they desperately need more computing power. These firms have ambitious growth plans, and if they stand up a new data center and have no chips to put in it, it's a waste of time. So, these companies are likely sharing their five-year plans and growth trajectories with Nvidia so that it can properly size its supply chain to provide them computing units when they need them. This gives Nvidia visibility into multiple years of growth and gives Huang the confidence he needs to issue a bold proclamation like that. We're already seeing evidence of Nvidia's comfort in forecasting revenue well ino the future, as the company issued guidance for 70% revenue growth for fiscal year (FY) 2028 (ending January 2028, encompassing most of 2027). That guidance was given because Nvidia knows it's likely maximizing its production rates next year, and it won't be able to deliver much better growth than that. While demand beyond FY 2028 isn't as clear, it's still visible enough for Nvidia to issue its full projection. But what does that mean for the stock? The reality is that none of this monster growth to reach $3 trillion to $4 trillion in global data center capital expenditures annually is priced into Nvidia's stock. Nvidia trades for just 29 times trailing earnings right now -- a pretty cheap price tag considering its impressive growth. None of 2027's projected 70% growth is priced into the stock, let alone whatever it will see in 2028 and beyond. This could be a major advantage for long-term investors, and buying shares now could result in very strong returns. The reality is that Nvidia will be one of the best stocks to own over the next few years as AI build-outs ramp up, and that will result in many satisfied investors who buy the stock now. Nvidia tops the short list of best stocks to buy now, and I think investors will be highly rewarded by taking a position in the stock while it's still cheap. Keithen Drury has positions in Nvidia. title: Broadcom vs. Nvidia: The AI Revolution Is Big Enough for Both. Here's the Better Buy. - The Motley Fool
content: Nvidia and Broadcom are two of the best-positioned stocks for the continued AI infrastructure boom. Nvidia (NVDA +0.97%) and Broadcom (AVGO +0.73%) are two of the largest and best-positioned semiconductor companies for the artificial intelligence age. The AI infrastructure market is expanding rapidly, with Gartner recently projecting it will hit nearly $2 trillion in 2027. While Broadcom versus Nvidia is essentially a battle between off-the-shelf graphics processing units (GPUs) and custom AI application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs), the AI infrastructure market is more than big enough for both companies to be winners. However, let's dig in to see which chip stock looks like the better buy today. Nvidia has been the biggest AI infrastructure winner thus far, becoming the world's largest company in the process. However, the stock still looks attractive, with big growth opportunities still in front of it, and it is trading at a forward P/E of only 14.5 times fiscal 2028 (ending January 2028) analyst estimates. The company remains the king of AI, with its GPUs still the primary chips powering AI workloads. It is particularly strong in the AI model training market, as its CUDA software platform, on which most foundational AI code was written, continues to provide it with a wide moat. Nvidia also dominates the neocloud and enterprise markets, while Space Exploration Technologies has also decided to use its chips exclusively. That said, what makes the future most exciting for Nvidia is that the company has really transformed itself from just a GPU maker into a complete AI infrastructure company. Its networking portfolio lets it provide complete end-to-end server solutions, while its Arm Holdings-based central processing units (CPUs) and newer language processing units (LPUs) (which come from its Groq "acquisition") allow it to configure them for specific AI tasks, like inference or agentic AI. It has also made important acquisitions in the software space (SchedMD and Hugging Face) that help it orchestrate and distribute AI. Not to be overlooked, Nvidia has also locked up a huge amount of the scarce high bandwidth memory (HBM) supply that AI chips need to be packaged with so that they aren't sitting idle. This all but assures that it will remain the AI chip leader. Missed Nvidia in 2009? One of the most common ways they are doing this is through designing their own custom AI chips, especially for inference, where Nvidia's CUDA moat is not as deep. This is benefiting Broadcom, which is a leader in ASICs, which are purpose-built, hardwired chips. It provides important IP (intellectual property) and services to help turn its customers' chip designs into reality. It helped Alphabet develop its Tensor Processing Units (TPUs), which are considered the gold standard of AI ASICs. This is a huge driver, with both Anthropic and Alphabet now large and growing TPU customers. This has also led to other hyperscalers developing their own custom chips, including OpenAI and Meta Platforms. Overall, Broadcom sees its ASIC revenue doubling next fiscal year to $115 billion, then doubling again in fiscal 2028 (ending October 2028) to $230 billion. Its custom chip business also feeds into its networking business, where it provides key components that let servers transfer data quickly and efficiently distribute AI workloads. The stock currently trades at a forward P/E of under 19 times fiscal 2027 estimates, but that drops to below 12 times based on the fiscal 2028 consensus. title: Dan Ives Says Semiconductor Sell-Off Is ‘Way Overdone’ As AI Spending Fears Rattle NVDA, MU, SKHY, SNDK - TradingView
content: Semiconductor stocks extended their slide in morning trading on Tuesday as AI chip competition and AI spending concerns continued to weigh on the sector; however, according to Yorkville partner Dan Ives, the sell-off is “way overdone.” “I think there’s some nervousness on the memory stocks,” said Ives in an interview with CNBC. “I continue to think it’s way overdone relative to the sell-off.” SK Hynix (SKHY) was among the top trending tickers on Stocktwits at the time of writing. The stock fell more than 5% in pre-market trade, on track to extend its decline for a sixth straight session and hit an over one-month low. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around the shares remained in ‘bullish’ territory over the past day. The VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) dropped as much as 1.4% in pre-market trade, with Nvidia (NVDA) edging 0.8% lower. Investors were also watching Advanced Micro (AMD), Micron (MU), SanDisk (SNDK), Applied Materials (AMAT) and others for their continued slide. Why Dan Ives Says AI Chip Stocks Have Fallen Too Far According to Ives, the overall market is “jittery” in terms of worries about the AI built built and “some sort of slowdown.” He contended that around 5% to 10% of data centers may not end up happening, but noted that deals are accelerating and the demand supply ratio is 13:1. “It’s going to show up in earnings relative to the hyperscalers, relative to chip names,” Ives stated. In his opinion, the upcoming earnings season should help calm investors' nerves. Ives pegged Microsoft (MSFT), Nvidia, Palantir (PLTR) and CrowdStrike (CRWD) as his favorites among the AI trade. MSFT stock edged 0.18% higher in pre-market trade, while PLTR stock and CRWD shares both slipped around 0.5%. Microsoft bucked the broader sell off after Barclays raised its price target on the stock to $600 from $512, reiterating an 'Overweight' rating, as part of its third quarter (Q3) earnings preview for software stocks. On Meta (META), Ives reiterated that Muse was a “game changer.” According to Ives, the Zuckerberg-led company will continue to play “catch up” to Anthropic and OpenAI, which will only speed up the “AI arms race.” META stock also edged around 0.5% lower in pre-market trade. Nvidia (NVDA:NASDAQ) has said its share of China's AI accelerator market is effectively zero, but Chinese tech companies are still buying its hardware by the million. According to a Financial Times report published on October 13, Chinese groups have bought more than 1 million Nvidia gaming and workstation chips this year to cover a shortfall in AI computing power. These are products US export rules don't block, including the RTX Pro 6000D and RTX Pro 5000. They're slower than Huawei's Ascend 910C at most tasks, but they can handle simpler AI work such as the prefill stage of inference. For companies that can't get enough compute at home, that's good enough. The FT's numbers explain why. Industry insiders estimate China's domestic AI chip supply could reach about 3.5 million units this year (including roughly 1 million made overseas), while demand is expected to far exceed 5 million. Add Nvidia's million and the total still falls short. That gap is why Nvidia keeps showing up in China's AI buildout despite four years of US restrictions and Beijing's push for self-sufficiency. Spending is rising faster than supply. Combined capex at Alibaba, ByteDance, and Tencent could more than double to about Rmb700 billion ($104 billion) this year, and Morgan Stanley puts China's total 2026 spending on computing power at $193 billion, about 21% of the US figure. In fiscal 2026 (ended January 2026), Gaming revenue rose 41% to $16.04 billion, well above the $12.46 billion crypto-era peak of fiscal 2022. Professional Visualization, where the RTX Pro workstation cards book, jumped 70% to $3.19 billion, about 51% above its previous high. That year largely predates the purchases the FT describes, though, so those figures don't show how much of the growth came from Chinese AI buyers. Revenue from customers in China, including Hong Kong, came to $19.68 billion in fiscal 2026. Nvidia reported $4.6 billion of first-quarter H20 sales before April's licensing requirement disrupted shipments, followed by approximately $60 million under licenses granted in August. Its disclosures don't break out the product mix of the remaining China revenue. Revenue from customers headquartered in China, including Hong Kong, reached $7.88 billion in the July quarter, roughly double a year earlier. The obvious objection is scale, and it's a fair one. Data Center revenue hit $89 billion in the July quarter, about 92% of Nvidia's $96.2 billion total, while China was only around 8%. A million gaming and workstation cards matter to China's AI labs far more than they matter to Nvidia's income statement. The fiscal 2026 data can't settle the question, since it mostly predates this year's buying and overlaps with a global gaming upgrade cycle. The July quarter is the better test, and China's doubling there points the same way as the FT. The more useful insight sits elsewhere. Nvidia's guidance still assumes no China data center compute revenue, and Chinese demand is reaching its top-end chips anyway, just not through China. That side door runs through Oracle (ORCL:NYSE). Last month, it has also been reported that Tencent signed an agreement to lease access to approximately 100,000 advanced AI chips through Oracle's Southeast Asian data centers. Such contracts can generate Oracle cloud revenue and support demand for Nvidia hardware outside China. Tencent (TCEHY) and Alibaba (BABA:NYSE) are the spenders behind this demand. Both are pushing new models and agent tools this year, and alongside ByteDance they're chasing offshore leases for the training work that workaround cards can't do. China's own chipmakers, led by Huawei and Cambricon (688256.SS:SHANGHAI), more than doubled domestic AI chip output this year and still left a gap of over a million chips. Until that closes, Nvidia stays in China's AI buildout through the back door, and Oracle is the clearest US beneficiary named in the FT's report. Immunovant is developing IMVT-1402 in an ongoing mid-stage study in Sjögren’s disease. Argenx’s efgartigimod works the same way: it lowers circulating IgG antibodies that can drive autoimmune disease. A late-stage failure for a closely related drug raises the odds that simply reducing IgG may not be enough in Sjögren’s. The move also follows Immunovant’s late-September setback, when IMVT-1402 missed its main goal in a cutaneous lupus study, and that program was dropped. Roivant is the majority owner of Immunovant, and IMVT-1402 is central to the group’s autoimmune story. Argenx has stopped its late-stage UNITY study of weekly subcutaneous efgartigimod in adults with moderate-to-severe Sjögren’s disease. An independent monitoring committee, after an interim look, said the trial was unlikely to meet its main goal: a reduction in systemic disease activity at week 48, the company said. Safety matched the drug’s known profile, with no new signals. Sjögren’s, which causes dry eyes, dry mouth, fatigue and joint pain, still has no approved targeted therapy and is unusually varied from patient to patient, which makes trials hard to win. title: $10,000 Invested Equally in Alphabet and Nvidia Could Be Worth This Much by 2030 - The Motley Fool
content: Split $10,000 between Alphabet and Nvidia today, and by 2030 that bet touches everything from search ads to robotaxis to quantum chips. Pick almost any frontier of anything from modern tech, search, or advertising, cloud computing, self-driving cars, or quantum physics, and odds are Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOGL) (GOOG +0.16%) or Nvidia (NVDA +0.97%) is already standing in it. Split $10,000 between the two today, and you aren't just buying a search engine and a chipmaker. You are betting that the next five years of computing will be built largely on top of what these two companies are shipping right now. Nvidia's second-quarter data center revenue hit $89 billion, up 117% from a year earlier. Data center revenue is simply the money Nvidia makes selling chips to the massive server farms that power AI, the physical buildings packed with computers that run everything from ChatGPT to online search and AI features. That growth came largely from Blackwell Ultra, Nvidia's current flagship chip family, ramping into the build-outs of nearly every major cloud provider on earth, meaning companies like Amazon, Microsoft, and Alphabet are all buying Nvidia hardware to stock the data centers they rent out to businesses and AI developers. Nvidia has already moved past Blackwell in conversation, too. Its newer chip platform, called Vera Rubin, is now in full production and promises up to 10 times lower cost per AI token than Blackwell delivered. In short, a token is roughly a chunk of text an AI model processes, so a lower cost per token means it gets meaningfully cheaper to run AI software at scale, which matters enormously for whether AI companies can eventually turn a profit. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has laid out a path to $1 trillion in cumulative sales from Blackwell and Rubin combined between 2025 and 2027 alone, according to The Information. That figure would have sounded like science fiction five years ago. Then there's another bet: quantum computing. Nvidia doesn't build quantum processors itself, but its NVQLink technology now connects quantum hardware directly to Nvidia's GPU supercomputers, and nearly every serious quantum player, from IonQ to national research labs, has started building on top of it. Alphabet's core advertising and search business remains the cash engine funding everything else, but "everything else" has gotten remarkably interesting. According to Tech Crunch, Waymo, Alphabet's self-driving unit, now completes 500,000 paid robotaxi rides every week across 10 U.S. cities, up tenfold in under two years, and it's targeting 1 million weekly rides across 20 cities by the end of 2026, including its first international markets. Waymo just upsized its first-ever debt offering to $5 billion specifically to fund that global expansion, a sign Alphabet is treating this less like a moonshot experiment and more like a business it intends to scale aggressively. On the quantum side, Alphabet's Willow chip completed a benchmark computation in under five minutes that would take today's fastest supercomputers an estimated 10 septillion years, a number so large it stops meaning anything useful except "a lot." Google has begun offering early access to Willow to external researchers, a step toward figuring out what a chip that fast is actually good for commercially.  Layer Gemini's ongoing push into search, cloud, and enterprise AI tools on top of that, and Alphabet looks like a conglomerate that happens to also sell ads. Alphabet trades around $354 per share, and Nvidia sits closer to $230 per share. Split $10,000 evenly between them, $5,000 each, and that buys roughly 14.1 shares of Alphabet and about 21.8 shares of Nvidia. Nothing fancy there, just simple division, but it's worth actually doing the math rather than treating these as abstract tickers, because 14 shares of one company and 22 of another is a very different feeling than a lump sum sitting in an account. Where this gets fun is projecting forward. Picture a steadier path first: Alphabet climbing to around $450 a share by 2030 as its cloud and AI businesses keep maturing, and Nvidia reaching roughly $500 as the Blackwell-to-Rubin transition plays out reasonably well. Under that scenario, the original $10,000 grows to somewhere around $17,245, not a moonshot, but a healthy return for five years of patience. Now picture the more optimistic version, the one where Waymo's robotaxi expansion actually hits its stride, Nvidia's quantum partnerships start paying off, and both companies keep compounding closer to their best-case potential. Alphabet near $650 and Nvidia near $900 would push that same $10,000 up toward $28,785, nearly triple the original stake. It's easy for me to say this. Remember, Nvidia's valuation already assumes years of AI spending keep accelerating, and Alphabet faces its own regulatory overhang from years of antitrust scrutiny in both the U.S. and Europe. Betting on both doesn't eliminate that risk; it just diversifies which frontier-tech story has to keep working. Micah Zimmerman has no position in any of the stocks mentioned. Hewlett Packard Enterprise HPE has partnered with NVIDIA NVDA to help enterprises and other large AI customers simplify and scale generative AI, agentic AI and high-performance computing workloads. The integration enables Hewlett Packard Enterprise to provide integrated AI infrastructure, including hardware, software and cloud management. At the core of the collaboration is HPE AI Factory with NVIDIA, a turnkey AI infrastructure solution that combines HPE's compute, storage, networking and GreenLake platform with NVIDIA's GPUs, CPUs, networking technologies and AI Enterprise software. The integrated offering allows enterprises to build and manage AI environments through a unified platform. The companies have also jointly engineered HPE Private Cloud AI, which enables customers to deploy generative AI and agentic AI applications securely in on-premises or hybrid cloud environments. The solution comes with pre-integrated hardware and software, reducing deployment complexity while providing enterprise-grade capabilities. HPE is further strengthening its AI hardware portfolio with AI-optimized servers such as the HPE ProLiant Compute DL394 Gen12, powered by NVIDIA's Vera CPU for reinforcement learning, AI agents, inference and large-scale data processing. The company also offers systems based on NVIDIA's Blackwell and Rubin architectures. To accelerate AI workloads, HPE integrates NVIDIA's Blackwell, HGX and RTX Pro GPUs alongside Spectrum-X Ethernet, InfiniBand networking, BlueField DPUs and ConnectX SuperNICs across its AI infrastructure portfolio. HPE also incorporates NVIDIA Agent Toolkit, Nemotron models, NeMo and OpenShell into HPE Private Cloud AI, enabling enterprises to build, govern and monitor AI agents with enhanced security and observability. HPE competes with Super Micro Computer SMCI and Dell Technologies DELL in the AI infrastructure space. Both SMCI and DELL are collaborating with NVIDIA to strengthen their offerings. For instance, Super Micro Computer's competitive advantage lies in its modular Building Block architecture that enables rapid product customization by reusing components across thousands of server configurations. Supported by more than 3,200 research and development engineers, SMCI quickly integrates new processors from NVIDIA, AMD, Intel and ARM. This rapid product development shortens time-to-market, lowers engineering costs and enables faster global shipments, making Super Micro Computer particularly attractive for customers seeking immediate AI deployment. Dell Technologies, meanwhile, is pursuing a broader ecosystem strategy through its Dell AI Factory with NVIDIA. Rather than focusing solely on servers, DELL is expanding across compute, storage, networking, automation and software. Dell Technologies recently introduced PowerEdge R9822 and M9822 servers powered by NVIDIA Vera CPUs for Agentic AI workloads. Yet the market now pays far less for each dollar of its expected profit than it did, on average, over the past five years. Something has to give. Either the earnings engine is about to stall, or the stock's discount is out of date. For anyone who hasn't followed the story, Nvidia designs the chips and systems that train and run artificial intelligence models. Its graphics processors started out in gaming PCs, but today the money comes overwhelmingly from data centers run by cloud giants, AI labs, and governments. It increasingly sells entire racks of processors, networking gear, and software rather than individual chips. Which is it? For investors weighing companies featured among 10 Best Return on Equity (ROE) Stocks to Buy, the answer depends less on Nvidia's record results than on whether its biggest customers can keep paying for them. Nvidia's edge is the whole stack. Developers have spent years building on its CUDA software platform, and moving to a rival means rewriting code and re-tuning systems. That switching cost keeps buyers loyal even as competitors improve. The numbers back it up. In fiscal Q2 2027 (ended in late July), Data Center revenue hit $89.0 billion, up 117% from a year earlier. GAAP gross margin reached 75.0%, compared with 72.4% in the year-ago quarter. A company losing its grip on customers usually has to cut prices; Nvidia's margins went the other way, reflecting the formidable pricing power and balance sheet strength showcased among 10 Stocks With Low Debt and Strong Free Cash Flow. The newest proof is the Vera Rubin platform, which Nvidia says is now in full production. Rubin racks are already running at CoreWeave, Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, and Nebius. Total revenue reached $96.2 billion in fiscal Q2, up 106% year over year and 18% from the prior quarter. Management guided fiscal Q3 revenue to $108.0 billion, plus or minus 2%. That outlook assumes no Data Center compute revenue from China, so any reopening there would be extra. Nvidia is also pushing into new territory, with its Vera CPU built for AI agents and the Groq 3 LPX inference accelerator (a chip for running models rather than training them) in full production. The moat looks wider, not narrower. Here's the catch. According to CNBC, Nvidia, Oracle, CoreWeave, and other AI stocks fell recently after a report on OpenAI's revenue. That reaction gets at the core worry: a small group of buyers is spending enormous sums well ahead of the revenue AI might eventually generate. Nvidia is even helping finance the buildout. It has set up compute financing platforms with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs, and KKR, aiming to mobilize more than $500 billion in third-party capital, subject to definitive agreements. Bulls see that as clearing a bottleneck. Skeptics see a supplier propping up its own demand, a question that hangs even more heavily over specialized AI cloud providers. For now, navigating this deployment payoff remains the main risk to watch across the 11 Best Agentic AI Stocks to Buy Right Now. At a forward P/E of 24.62, as of October 9, investors are paying roughly $25 for every $1 of expected earnings. That's well below Nvidia's 5-year average of 42.13 and only a whisker above the sector's 23.35. Now set that against growth. Adjusted EPS (which excludes items Nvidia treats as outside day-to-day operations) came in at $2.22 in fiscal Q2, up from $1.01 a year earlier. GAAP EPS was higher at $2.46, but the adjusted figure gives the cleaner read on the core business. Looking further out, expected EPS growth stands at 70.90% in 2028. A company growing that quickly would normally command a premium to its sector, not near-parity. The market is effectively pricing in a sharp slowdown, which ties straight back to the customer-spending worry. That near-sector multiple also invites comparison with the foundry that manufactures its chips, highlighting why it remains closely watched alongside the other 10 Best AI Stocks to Buy Before They Explode. Professional money hasn't been scared off. Hedge fund interest ticked up, with 285 funds holding the stock in the most recent quarter, up from 275 in the prior one. Short interest sits at just 1.27% of the float, a sign of relatively limited bearish positioning. The evidence points to a business whose moat is widening while its valuation assumes the opposite. If Rubin keeps ramping and fiscal Q3 lands within its own outlook range, a multiple near the sector's looks hard to defend for long. That setup suits investors with a multiyear horizon who can stomach sharp swings tied to AI spending headlines. What would change the picture is clear: a pullback in spending by the big AI labs and cloud providers, or gross margin slipping meaningfully below the roughly 74% Nvidia has guided for. While we acknowledge the risk and potential of NVDA as an investment, our conviction lies in the belief that some AI stocks hold greater promise for delivering higher returns and doing so within a shorter time frame. Nvidia Corp (NASDAQ:NVDA, XETRA:NVD) shares fell 1% to $226.55, down $2.73, after Microsoft Corp (NASDAQ:MSFT) unveiled a new artificial intelligence chip that threatens to reduce its reliance on the graphics processor maker. Microsoft, the software and cloud computing giant, introduced its third-generation Maia 300 processor on Monday, targeting lower costs and greater efficiency in running AI workloads across its products and services. The chip is designed to deliver 40% more tokens per megawatt than leading graphics processing unit (GPU) systems, with a configuration of 96 accelerators offering up to seven times the rack-scale throughput of its predecessor, Maia 200. Microsoft plans to begin deploying Maia 300 in production workloads in 2027 and scale its in-house chip programme to multi-gigawatt deployments, making Maia its primary system for AI inference, the process of running trained models to generate responses. The move presents a potential competitive challenge for Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices, whose processors have supplied much of the hardware used to run AI services, as cloud providers seek greater control over infrastructure costs and performance. Microsoft already uses Maia 200 in production, including for Microsoft Copilot, and plans to extend its deployment across additional services as it develops its own AI models and infrastructure. The Maia 300 uses a chiplet architecture built around Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company's advanced manufacturing technology, separating computing, memory control and input-output functions to improve efficiency. Nvidia's broader market position will depend on whether demand for AI computing continues to expand enough to offset customers developing their own alternatives, while Microsoft's planned rollout remains more than a year away.
